passages.original: sero igitur a nostris poëtae vel cogniti vel recepti. quamquam est in Originibus solitos esse in epulis canere convivas ad tibicinem de clarorum hominum virtutibus; honorem tamen huic generi non fuisse declarat oratio Catonis, in qua obiecit ut probrum M. Nobiliori, quod is in provinciam poëtas duxisset; duxerat autem consul ille in Aetoliam, ut scimus, Ennium. quo minus igitur honoris erat poëtis, eo minora studia fuerunt, nec tamen, si qui magnis ingeniis in eo genere extiterunt,
passages.english: Poets, then, were recognized or received by our people late. And yet it is stated in the Origins that guests at banquets used to sing to the pipe about the virtues of famous men; that there was no honour for this class, however, is shown by a speech of Cato, in which he reproached Marcus Nobilior as a disgrace for having taken poets with him into his province; and that consul had, as we know, taken Ennius into Aetolia. So the less honour there was for poets, the smaller the enthusiasm [for poetry] was; and yet, if any men of great talent arose in that field,
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence. 'Origins' is Cato's historical work.

passages.original: Sed ut Aristoteles, vir summo ingenio, scientia, copia, cum motus esset Isocratis rhetoris gloria, dicere docere etiam coepit adulescentes et prudentiam cum eloquentia iungere, sic nobis placet nec pristinum dicendi studium deponere et in hac maiore et uberiore arte versari.
passages.english: But just as Aristotle, a man of the highest talent, knowledge and fluency, when he had been stirred by the fame of the rhetorician Isocrates, also began to teach young men to speak and to join wisdom with eloquence, so I too resolve neither to lay aside my former devotion to oratory and to occupy myself in this greater and richer art.
passages.notes: The Latin 'nec ... et' (literally 'neither to lay aside ... and to occupy myself') is an idiomatic pairing meaning 'not to lay aside ... and yet to occupy myself'.

passages.original: quid sit porro ipse animus aut ubi aut unde, magna dissensio est. aliis cor ipsum animus videtur, ex quo excordes, vecordes concordesque dicuntur et Nasica ille prudens bis consul Corculum et egregie cordatus homo, catus Aelius Sextus. Empedocles animum esse censet cordi suffusum sanguinem; aliis pars quaedam cerebri visa est animi principatum tenere; aliis nec cor ipsum placet nec cerebri quandam partem esse animum,
passages.english: Further, what the soul itself is, or where, or whence, is a matter of great disagreement. To some the heart itself seems to be the soul, from which [people] are called 'excordes' (heartless), 'vecordes' (senseless) and 'concordes' (of one heart), and that wise Nasica, twice consul, [was called] 'Corculum' (Little Heart), and 'an outstandingly hearted man, shrewd Aelius Sextus.' Empedocles holds that the soul is the blood suffused around the heart; to others a certain part of the brain has seemed to hold the sovereignty of the soul; others approve neither that the heart itself nor some part of the brain is the soul,
passages.notes: The Latin wordplay on cor (heart) is glossed in parentheses. 'egregie cordatus homo, catus Aelius Sextus' is a quotation of Ennius. The passage breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: nam si cor aut sanguis aut cerebrum est animus, certe, quoniam est corpus, interibit cum reliquo corpore; si anima est, fortasse dissipabitur; si ignis, extinguetur; si est Aristoxeni harmonia, dissolvetur. quid de Dicaearcho dicam, qui nihil omnino animum dicat esse? his sententiis omnibus nihil post mortem pertinere ad quemquam potest; pariter enim cum vita sensus amittitur; non sentientis autem nihil est ullam in partem quod intersit. reliquorum sententiae spem adferunt, si te hoc forte delectat, posse animos, cum e corporibus excesserint, in caelum quasi in domicilium suum pervenire.
passages.english: For if the soul is the heart or blood or brain, then certainly, since it is body, it will perish with the rest of the body; if it is breath, it will perhaps be dispersed; if fire, it will be extinguished; if it is Aristoxenus' harmony, it will be dissolved. What shall I say of Dicaearchus, who says that the soul is nothing at all? On all these views nothing after death can concern anyone; for sensation is lost together with life, and for one who does not feel there is nothing that makes any difference in any direction. The views of the rest offer hope, if this perhaps pleases you, that souls, when they have left their bodies, can reach heaven as if their own home.
passages.notes: anima: 'breath' or 'air'.

passages.original: Itaque unum illud erat insitum priscis illis, quos cascos appellat Ennius, esse in morte sensum neque excessu vitae sic deleri hominem, ut funditus interiret;
passages.english: And so this one thing was implanted in those ancients, whom Ennius calls 'cascei' (men of old): that there is sensation in death, and that a man is not so destroyed by departing from life that he perishes utterly;

passages.original: ex hoc et nostrorum opinione Romulus in caelo cum diis agit aevum, ut famae adsentiens dixit Ennius, et apud Graecos indeque perlapsus ad nos et usque ad Oceanum Hercules tantus et tam praesens habetur deus; hinc Liber Semela natus eademque famae celebritate Tyndaridae fratres, qui non modo adiutores in proeliis victoriae populi Romani, sed etiam nuntii fuisse perhibentur.
passages.english: from this, and from the belief of our people, Romulus 'passes his age in heaven with the gods', as Ennius said, agreeing with tradition; and among the Greeks, and from there gliding down to us and as far as the Ocean, Hercules is held to be so great and so ever-present a god; hence Liber, born of Semele, and with the same widespread fame the Tyndarid brothers, who are said to have been not only helpers of the Roman people toward victory in battles but also messengers [of it].
passages.notes: Liber = Bacchus/Dionysus; the Tyndarid brothers = Castor and Pollux.

passages.original: Maxumum vero argumentum est naturam ipsam de inmortalitate animorum tacitam iudicare, quod omnibus curae sunt, et maxumae quidem, quae post mortem futura sint.serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint, ut ait Statius in Synephebis, quid spectans nisi etiam postera saecula ad se pertinere? ergo arbores seret diligens agricola, quarum aspiciet bacam ipse numquam; vir magnus leges instituta rem publicam non seret?
passages.english: But the greatest proof is that nature herself silently judges in favour of the immortality of souls, in that all people care, and indeed care very greatly, about what will happen after death. "He plants trees to benefit another generation," as Statius says in the Synephebi; with what in view, unless [he thinks] that later generations also concern him? So the diligent farmer will plant trees whose fruit he himself will never see; and will a great man not plant laws, institutions, the commonwealth?
passages.notes: Statius here is the comic poet Caecilius Statius; the Synephebi is his comedy. Missing space in 'sint.serit' corrected.

passages.original: haec enim pulchritudo etiam in terris patritam illam et avitam, ut ait Theophrastus, philosophiam cognitionis cupiditate incensam excitavit. praecipue vero fruentur ea, qui tum etiam, cum has terras incolentes circumfusi erant caligine, tamen acie mentis dispicere cupiebant.
passages.english: For it was this beauty that, even on earth, roused that philosophy 'of our fathers and grandfathers', as Theophrastus calls it, kindled by the desire for knowledge. But those will enjoy it most who even then, while they dwelt on this earth surrounded by darkness, nevertheless longed to see through it with the keenness of the mind.
passages.notes: 'patritam illam et avitam' is a quoted phrase attributed to Theophrastus, 'ancestral and inherited'.

passages.original: praeclarum autem nescio quid adepti sunt, quod didicerunt se, cum tempus mortis venisset, totos esse perituros. quod ut ita sit —nihil enim pugno—, quid habet ista res aut laetabile aut gloriosum? Nec tamen mihi sane quicquam occurrit, cur non Pythagorae sit et Platonis vera sententia. ut enim rationem Plato nullam adferret—vide, quid homini tribuam—, ipsa auctoritate me frangeret: tot autem rationes attulit, ut velle ceteris, sibi certe persuasisse videatur.
passages.english: But they have gained something splendid, I suppose, in having learned that when the time of death comes they will perish entirely. Granted that this is so (for I do not fight it), what does that thing have that is either gladdening or glorious? And yet nothing at all occurs to me why the view of Pythagoras and Plato should not be true. For even if Plato offered no argument (see how much I grant the man), he would overpower me by his authority alone; but he has offered so many arguments that he seems to have wanted to persuade others, and certainly to have persuaded himself.
passages.notes: The first sentence is ironic.

passages.original: cumque nihil esset , ut omnibus locis a Platone disseritur—nihil enim putat esse, quod oriatur et intereat, idque solum esse, quod semper tale sit quale est (ἰδέαν appellat ille, nos speciem)—, non potuit animus haec in corpore inclusus adgnoscere, cognita attulit; ex quo tam multarum rerum cognitionis admiratio tollitur.
passages.english: And since nothing existed [for the soul to learn from in the body], as Plato argues everywhere (for he thinks that nothing that comes into being and perishes truly exists, and that only that exists which is always such as it is; he calls it idea, we call it species [form]), the soul, shut up in the body, could not have come to know these things; it brought them already known. From this the wonder at the knowledge of so many things is removed.
passages.notes: The text after 'cumque nihil esset' seems to lack words (e.g. 'in vita' or similar); the bracketed supplement is conjectural. Greek ἰδέαν kept as 'idea'.

passages.original: Mihi vero ne haec quidem notiora et inlustriora carere vi divina videntur, ut ego aut poëtam grave plenumque carmen sine caelesti aliquo mentis instinctu putem fundere, aut eloquentiam sine maiore quadam vi fluere abundantem sonantibus verbis uberibusque sententiis. philosophia vero, omnium mater artium, quid est aliud nisi, ut Plato, donum, ut ego, inventum deorum? haec nos primum ad illorum cultum, deinde ad ius hominum, quod situm est in generis humani societate, tum ad modestiam magnitudinemque animi erudivit, eademque ab animo tamquam ab oculis caliginem dispulit, ut omnia supera infera prima ultima media videremus.
passages.english: To me, indeed, not even these more familiar and more conspicuous things seem to lack divine power, so that I could think either that a poet pours forth a weighty and full song without some heavenly inspiration of the mind, or that eloquence flows abundantly with resounding words and rich thoughts without some greater power. And philosophy, the mother of all the arts, what is it but, as Plato says, a gift, or, as I say, an invention of the gods? She has trained us first to their worship, then to the justice due among men, which is grounded in the fellowship of the human race, and then to moderation and greatness of mind; and she has likewise driven darkness from the mind as if from the eyes, so that we might see all things above and below, first, last and in between.
passages.notes: 'ut ego ... putem' is consecutive with a negative force: 'so that I could not think'; sense: I cannot believe a poet composes without inspiration.

passages.original: non iusta causa, cur Laomedonti tanta fieret iniuria. fingebat haec Homerus et humana ad deos transferebat: divina mallem ad nos. quae autem divina? vigere, sapere, invenire, meminisse. ergo animus qui ..., ut ego dico, divinus est, ut Euripides dicere audet, deus. Et quidem, si deus aut anima aut ignis est, idem est animus hominis. nam ut illa natura caelestis et terra vacat et umore, sic utriusque harum rerum humanus animus est expers;
passages.english: [there was] no just cause why so great a wrong should be done to Laomedon. Homer invented these things and transferred human traits to the gods; I would rather [he had transferred] divine traits to us. But what are divine traits? To be active, to be wise, to discover, to remember. Therefore the soul, which [...], is, as I say, divine, and, as Euripides dares to say, a god. And indeed, if god is either air or fire, so is the soul of man. For just as that heavenly nature is free of earth and moisture, so the human soul has no share in either of these things;
passages.notes: There is a lacuna after 'animus qui' in the edition. 'anima' here means air/breath.

passages.original: haec igitur et alia innumerabilia cum cernimus, possumusne dubitare quin is praesit aliquis vel effector, si haec nata sunt, ut Platoni videtur, vel, si semper fuerunt, ut Aristoteli placet, moderator tanti operis et muneris? sic mentem hominis, quamvis eam non videas, ut deum non vides, tamen, ut deum adgnoscis ex operibus eius, sic ex memoria rerum et inventione et celeritate motus omnique pulchritudine virtutis vim divinam mentis adgnoscito.
passages.english: When, then, we behold these and countless other things, can we doubt that some being presides over them, either a maker, if they came into being, as Plato thinks, or, if they have always existed, as Aristotle holds, a governor of so great a work and task? So the mind of man, although you do not see it, just as you do not see god, nevertheless, as you recognise god from his works, so from its memory of things, its power of discovery, the swiftness of its movement, and all the beauty of its virtue, recognise the divine power of the mind.

passages.original: sed haec et vetera et a Graecis; Cato autem sic abiit e vita, ut causam moriendi nactum se esse gauderet. vetat enim dominans ille in nobis deus iniussu hinc nos suo demigrare; cum vero causam iustam deus ipse dederit, ut tunc Socrati, nunc Catoni, saepe multis, ne ille me Dius Fidius vir sapiens laetus ex his tenebris in lucem illam excesserit, nec tamen ille vincla carceris ruperit—leges enim vetant—, sed tamquam a magistratu aut ab aliqua potestate legitima, sic a deo evocatus atque emissus exierit.
passages.english: But these things are both old and from the Greeks; Cato, however, departed from life in such a way that he rejoiced at having found a reason for dying. For that god who rules in us forbids us to depart from here without his command; but when the god himself has given a just cause, as once to Socrates, now to Cato, and often to many, then truly, by Dius Fidius, that wise man will gladly have passed out of this darkness into that light; and yet he will not have broken the chains of his prison — for the laws forbid it — but, as if summoned and released by a magistrate or some lawful authority, so called forth and released by the god, he will have gone out.
passages.notes: 'ne ille me Dius Fidius' is an oath formula ('so help me Dius Fidius'); 'ne' here is the affirmative particle.

passages.original: Bene reprehendis, et se isto modo res habet. credamus igitur Panaetio a Platone suo dissentienti? quem enim omnibus locis divinum, quem sapientissimum, quem sanctissimum, quem Homerum philosophorum appellat, huius hanc unam sententiam de inmortalitate animorum non probat. volt enim, quod nemo negat, quicquid natum sit interire; nasci autem animos, quod declaret eorum similitudo qui procreentur, quae etiam in ingeniis, non solum in corporibus appareat.
passages.english: You rightly rebuke [me], and that is how the matter stands. Shall we then believe Panaetius when he disagrees with his Plato? For the man whom everywhere he calls divine, most wise, most holy, the Homer of philosophers, of him he rejects this one view on the immortality of souls. For he holds, which no one denies, that whatever has been born perishes; and that souls are born, as is shown by the likeness of those who are begotten [to their parents], which appears in their characters too, not only in their bodies.
passages.notes: 'se isto modo' is likely a scanning error for 'sic isto modo' or 'se ... habet'; sense unaffected.

passages.original: iam similitudo magis apparet in bestiis, quarum animi sunt rationis expertes; hominum autem similitudo in corporum figura magis exstat, et ipsi animi magni refert quali in corpore locati sint. multa enim e corpore existunt, quae acuant mentem, multa, quae obtundant. Aristoteles quidem ait omnis ingeniosos melancholicos esse, ut ego me tardiorem esse non moleste feram. enumerat multos, idque quasi constet, rationem cur ita fiat adfert. quod si tanta vis est ad habitum mentis in is quae gignuntur in corpore, ea sunt autem, quaecumque sunt, quae similitudinem faciant, nihil necessitatis adfert, cur nascantur animi, similitudo.
passages.english: Moreover, likeness is more apparent in animals, whose minds are without reason; while among humans likeness stands out more in bodily form, and it matters greatly to minds themselves in what sort of body they are placed. For many things arise from the body which sharpen the mind, and many which blunt it. Aristotle indeed says that all gifted people are melancholic, so that I do not mind being somewhat slow-witted. He lists many, and, as if it were established, he gives the reason why this happens. But if the things produced in the body have so much power over the state of the mind, and it is these, whatever they are, that produce likeness, then likeness supplies no necessary reason why minds should be born.
passages.notes: 'in is' = 'in iis'.

passages.original: sed fac, ut isti volunt, animos non remanere post mortem: video nos, si ita sit, privari spe beatioris vitae; mali vero quid adfert ista sententia? fac enim sic animum interire ut corpus: num igitur aliquis dolor aut omnino post mortem sensus in corpore est? nemo id quidem dicit, etsi Democritum insimulat Epicurus, Democritii negant. ne in animo quidem igitur sensus remanet; ipse enim nusquam est. ubi igitur malum est, quoniam nihil tertium est? an quod ipse animi discessus a corpore non fit sine dolore? ut credam ita esse, quam est id exiguum!
passages.english: But suppose, as they would have it, that souls do not survive after death: I see that, if so, we are deprived of the hope of a happier life; but what evil does that view bring? For suppose the soul perishes just like the body: is there then any pain, or any sensation at all, in the body after death? No one says so, although Epicurus accuses Democritus [of it], while the Democriteans deny it. Then neither does sensation remain in the soul; for the soul itself is nowhere. Where then is the evil, since there is no third possibility? Or is it because the very departure of the soul from the body does not happen without pain? Even if I were to believe that this is so, how slight a thing it is!

passages.original: nondum gustaverat, inquit, vitae suavitatem; hic autem iam sperabat magna, quibus frui coeuperat. at id quidem in ceteris rebus melius putatur, aliquam partem quam nullam attingere: cur in vita secus? (quamquam non male ait Callimachus multo saepius lacrimasse Priamum quam Troilum). eorum autem, qui exacta aetate moriuntur, fortuna laudatur.
passages.english: "He had not yet tasted," they say, "the sweetness of life; but this one was already hoping for great things, which he had begun to enjoy." Yet in other matters it is thought better to attain some part than none: why otherwise in life? (Although Callimachus says, not badly, that Priam wept far more often than Troilus.) But the fortune of those who die when their life has run its full course is praised.
passages.notes: "coeuperat" read as "coeperat".

passages.original: sed quia ultra nihil habemus, hoc longum dicimus. Omnia ista, perinde ut cuique data sunt pro rata parte, ita aut longa aut brevia dicuntur. apud Hypanim fluvium, qui ab Europae parte in Pontum influit, Aristoteles ait bestiolas quasdam nasci, quae unum diem vivant. ex his igitur hora VIII quae mortua est, provecta aetate mortua est; quae vero occidente sole, decrepita, eo magis, si etiam solstitiali die. confer nostram longissimam aetatem cum aeternitate: in eadem propemodum brevitate qua illae bestiolae reperiemur.
passages.english: But because we have nothing beyond it, we call this long. All these things are called either long or short according to the proportion in which they have been given to each. By the river Hypanis, which flows into the Pontus from the European side, Aristotle says certain little creatures are born which live for one day. Of these, then, the one that has died at the eighth hour has died at an advanced age; the one that dies at sunset, in decrepitude, and all the more so if it is also on the day of the solstice. Compare our longest lifetime with eternity: we shall be found in almost the same brevity as those little creatures.

passages.original: sed quid duces et principes nominem, cum legiones scribat Cato saepe alacris in eum locum profectas, unde redituras se non arbitrarentur? pari animo Lacedaemonii in Thermopylis occiderunt, in quos Simonides: Dic, hospes, Spartae nos te hic vidisse iacentis,Dum sanctis patriae legibus obsequimur. quid ille dux Leonidas dicit?pergite animo forti, Lacedaemonii, hodie apud inferos fortasse cenabimus. fuit haec gens fortis, dum Lycurgi leges vigebant.
passages.english:
But why should I name generals and leaders, when Cato writes that legions often set out eagerly for a place from which they did not think they would return? With equal spirit the Spartans fell at Thermopylae, about whom Simonides [wrote]:
'Tell Sparta, stranger, that you saw us lying here,
while we obey the sacred laws of our fatherland.'
What does that leader Leonidas say? 'Go forward with brave spirit, Spartans; today perhaps we shall dine among the dead.' This was a brave race, while the laws of Lycurgus flourished.

passages.original: Neu réliquias semésas sireis dénudatis óssibus Per térram sanie délibutas foéde divexárier— non intellego, quid metuat, cum tam bonos septenarios fundat ad tibiam. Tenendum est igitur nihil curandum esse post mortem, cum multi inimicos etiam mortuos poeniuntur. exsecratur luculentis sane versibus apud Ennium Thyestes, primum ut naufragio pereat Atreus: durum hoc sane; talis enim interitus non est sine gravi sensu; illa inania: Ipse summis sáxis fixus ásperis, evísceratus,Látere pendens, sáxa spargens tábo, sanie et sánguine atro—
passages.english:
'...nor that you let my half-eaten remains, with bones laid bare, be foully dragged about the earth, smeared with gore—' I do not understand what he fears, when he pours out such fine septenarii to the pipe. We must hold, then, that nothing need be cared about after death, though many even punish their enemies when dead. In quite splendid verses in Ennius, Thyestes curses, first that Atreus may perish by shipwreck: this is certainly harsh, for such a death is not without severe sensation; but these are empty:
'He himself, pinned on rough, lofty rocks, disembowelled,
hanging by his side, spattering the rocks with gore, pus and black blood—'
passages.notes: 'sireis' read as 'siris' (you allow). 'poeniuntur' = puniuntur (archaic form).

passages.original: Deorum inmortalium iudicia solent in scholis proferre de morte, nec vero ea fingere ipsi, sed Herodoto auctore aliisque pluribus. primum Argiae sacerdotis Cleobis et Bito filii praedicantur. nota fabula est. cum enim illam ad sollemne et statutum sacrificium curru vehi ius esset satis longe ab oppido ad fanum morarenturque iumenta, tum iuvenes i quos modo nominavi veste posita corpora oleo perunxerunt, ad iugum accesserunt.
passages.english: In the schools they are accustomed to bring forward the judgements of the immortal gods about death, and they do not invent these themselves, but have Herodotus and many others as authority. First, Cleobis and Biton, the sons of the Argive priestess, are celebrated. The story is well known. Since it was required that she be carried in a carriage to a solemn and appointed sacrifice, quite a long way from the town to the temple, and the draught animals were delayed, then the young men whom I have just named laid aside their clothing, anointed their bodies with oil, and went to the yoke.
passages.notes: "i" before "quos" taken as "ii" (or a stray mark).

passages.original: qua est sententia in Cresphonte usus Euripides:Nam nós decebat coétus celebrantís domum Lugére, ubi esset áliquis in lucem éditus,Humánae vitae vária reputantís mala;At, quí labores mórte finissét gravis,Hunc ómni amicos laúde et laetitia éxsequi.
passages.english:
Euripides used this idea in the Cresphontes:
For we ought to gather in assembly and fill the house
with mourning, when anyone has been brought forth into the light,
reflecting on the varied ills of human life;
but him who has ended heavy labours by death,
him his friends should escort to burial with every praise and with joy.

passages.original: Neoptolemus quidem apud Ennium philosophari sibi ait necesse esse, sed paucis; nam omnino haud placere: ego autem, Brute, necesse mihi quidem esse arbitror philosophari—nam quid possum, praesertim nihil agens, agere melius?—sed non paucis, ut ille.
passages.english: Neoptolemus, indeed, in Ennius says that he must philosophize, but in few words; for [to do so] wholly does not please him. But I, Brutus, think that I must indeed philosophize — for what better can I do, especially when I have nothing to do? — but not in few words, as he does.
passages.notes: 'paucis' may mean 'a little' / 'on a few points' rather than 'in few words'.

passages.original: nam, ut Platonem reliquosque Socraticos et deinceps eos, qui ab his profecti sunt, legunt omnes, etiam qui illa aut non adprobant aut non studiosissime consectantur, Epicurum autem et Metrodorum non fere praeter suos quisquam in manus sumit, sic hos Latinos i soli legunt, qui illa recte dici putant.
passages.english: For just as everyone reads Plato and the other Socratics, and in turn those who derived from them, even those who either do not approve of those doctrines or do not pursue them very zealously, while hardly anyone apart from their own followers takes Epicurus and Metrodorus in hand, so these Latin writers are read only by those who think those doctrines are rightly stated.
passages.notes: "i soli" read as "ii soli" or stray mark.

passages.original: Nullum vero id quidem argumentum est. nam ut agri non omnes frugiferi sunt qui coluntur, falsumque illud Acci:Probae étsi in segetem súnt deteriorém datae Frugés, tamen ipsae suápte natura énitent, sic animi non omnes culti fructum ferunt. atque, ut in eodem simili verser, ut ager quamvis fertilis sine cultura fructuosus esse non potest, sic sine doctrina animus;
passages.english:
That, however, is no argument at all. For just as not all fields that are cultivated are fruitful — and that line of Accius is false:
'Even if good seeds are sown in poorer soil,
still by their own nature they shine forth' —
so not all minds that are cultivated bear fruit. And, to stay with the same comparison, just as a field, however fertile, cannot be productive without cultivation, so neither can the mind without learning;

passages.original: Metrodorus quidem perfecte eum beatum putat, cui corpus bene constitutum sit et exploratum ita semper fore. quis autem est iste, cui id exploratum possit esse? Epicurus vero ea dicit, ut mihi quidem risus captare videatur. adfirmat enim quodam loco, si uratur sapiens, si crucietur—expectas fortasse, dum dicat: patietur, perferet, non succumbet; magna mehercule laus et eo ipso, per quem iuravi, Hercule, digna;
passages.english: Metrodorus indeed thinks that man perfectly happy whose body is in good condition and who is assured that it will always be so. But who is that man to whom this could be assured? Epicurus, however, says things such that he seems to me at least to be angling for laughs. For he asserts in a certain passage that if the wise man is burned, if he is tortured—you perhaps expect him to say: he will endure, he will bear it through, he will not give way; great praise, by Hercules, and worthy of the very one by whom I swore, Hercules;

passages.original: Sed videamus Herculem ipsum, qui tum dolore frangebatur, cum inmortalitatem ipsa morte quaerebat: quas hic voces apud Sophoclem in Trachiniis edit! cui cum Deianira sanguine Centauri tinctam tunicam induisset inhaesissetque ea visceribus, ait ille: 1046 O múlta dictu grávia, perpessu áspera,Quae córpore exancláta atque animo pértuli!Nec míhi Iunonis térror inplacábilis Nec tántum invexit trístis Eurystheús mali,1050 Quantum úna vaecors Oénei partu édita.Haec me ínretivit véste furiali ínscium,Quae látere inhaerens mórsu lacerat víscera Urgénsque graviter púlmonum haurit spíritus: Iam décolorem sánguinem omnem exórbuit.Sic córpus clade horríbili absumptum éxtabuit,Ipse ínligatus péste interimor téxtili.Hos nón hostilis déxtra, non Terra édita Molés Gigantum, nón biformato ímpetu Centaúrus ictus córpori inflixít meo,1060 Non Gráia vis, non bárbara ulla inmánitas,Non saéva terris géns relegata últimis,Quas péragrans undique ómnem ecferitatem éxpuli,Sed féminae vir féminea interimór manu.O náte, vere hoc nómen usurpá patri,Ne me óccidentem mátris superet cáritas.Huc árripe ad me mánibus abstractám piis;Iam cérnam, mene an íllam potiorém putes.
passages.english:
But let us look at Hercules himself, who was being broken by pain at the very time when he was seeking immortality by death itself: what cries he utters in Sophocles' Trachiniae! When Deianira had put on him a tunic dyed with the Centaur's blood and it had clung to his flesh, he says:
O many things grievous to tell, harsh to endure,
which I have borne to exhaustion in body and in mind!
Neither the implacable terror of Juno
nor grim Eurystheus brought on me so much evil
as one mad woman, born the child of Oeneus.
She has ensnared me, unknowing, in a maddening robe,
which clinging to my side tears my flesh with its bite
and, pressing hard, drains the breath of my lungs:
already it has sucked dry all my discoloured blood.
So my body, consumed by a horrible ruin, has wasted away;
I myself, bound fast, am being killed by a woven plague.
These blows no enemy's right hand, no earth-born
mass of Giants, no Centaur with his two-formed onrush
has inflicted on my body,
no Greek force, no barbarian savagery,
no fierce race banished to the ends of the earth,
wandering through which I drove out all wildness everywhere;
but I, a man, am being killed by a woman's hand.
O son, truly claim this name for your father,
and do not let love of your mother overcome [love for] me as I die.
Seize her and drag her here to me with dutiful hands;
now I shall see whether you think me or her more important.
passages.notes: Line numbers (1046, 1050, 1060) from the edition omitted.

passages.original: virtutis magistri, philosophi, inventi sunt, qui summum malum dolorem dicerent. at tu, adulescens, cum id tibi paulo ante dixisses videri, rogatus a me, etiamne maius quam dedecus, verbo de sententia destitisti. roga hoc idem Epicurum: maius dicet esse malum mediocrem dolorem quam maxumum dedecus; in ipso enim dedecore mali nihil esse, nisi sequantur dolores. quis igitur Epicurum sequitur dolor, cum hoc ipsum dicit, summum malum esse dolorem?
passages.english: Philosophers, teachers of virtue, have been found who said that pain is the greatest evil. But you, young man, though you had said a little earlier that this seemed so to you, when I asked whether it was greater even than disgrace, abandoned your opinion at a word. Ask Epicurus this same thing: he will say that moderate pain is a greater evil than the greatest disgrace; for in disgrace itself there is nothing evil, unless pains follow. What pain, then, follows Epicurus when he says this very thing, that pain is the greatest evil?

passages.original: quaerit enim, quid actum sit: Elóquere eloquere, rés Argivum proélio ut se sústinet.—Non pótest ecfari tántum dictis, quántum factis súppetit Labóris. quiesce igitur et volnus alliga. etiamsi Eurypylus posset, non posset Aesopus: Ubi fortuna Hectóris nostram acrem áciem inclinatám et cetera explicat in dolore; sic est enim intemperans militaris in forti viro gloria. ergo haec veteranus miles facere poterit, doctus vir sapiensque non poterit?
passages.english: For he asks what has happened: "Speak out, speak out, how the Argives' cause holds up in battle."—"It is not possible to express in words as much as there is of toil in deeds." Be quiet, then, and bind up the wound. Even if Eurypylus could, Aesopus could not: "When the fortune of Hector made our fierce line give way," and the rest he sets out in his pain; so unrestrained is military glory in a brave man. So then, will a veteran soldier be able to do these things, and a learned and wise man not be able to?
passages.notes: Aesopus is the Roman tragic actor; the sense of the contrast is somewhat elliptical.

passages.original: at et morbi perniciosiores pluresque sunt animi quam corporis; hi enim ipsi odiosi sunt, quod ad animum pertinent eumque sollicitant,animusque aeger, ut ait Ennius,semper errat neque pati neque perpeti potest, cupere numquam desinit. quibus duobus morbis, ut omittam alios, aegritudine et cupiditate, qui tandem possunt in corpore esse graviores? qui vero probari potest ut sibi mederi animus non possit, cum ipsam medicinam corporis animus invenerit, cumque ad corporum sanationem multum ipsa corpora et natura valeat nec omnes, qui curari se passi sint, continuo etiam convalescant, animi autem, qui se sanari voluerint praeceptisque sapientium paruerint, sine ulla dubitatione sanentur?
passages.english: But the diseases of the mind are both more destructive and more numerous than those of the body; for these very [diseases] are hateful because they concern the mind and trouble it, and "the sick mind," as Ennius says, "always wanders, and can neither endure nor bear out, and never ceases to desire." Than these two diseases, to pass over others, distress and desire, what diseases, pray, can there be in the body more grave? And how can it be accepted that the mind cannot heal itself, when it was the mind that discovered the very medicine of the body, and when, for the healing of bodies, the bodies themselves and nature have great power, and not all who have allowed themselves to be treated at once recover as well, whereas minds that have wished to be healed and have obeyed the precepts of the wise are healed beyond any doubt?

passages.original: Itaque non inscite Heracleotes Dionysius ad ea disputat, quae apud Homerum Achilles queritur hoc, ut opinor, modo: Corque meum penitus turgescit tristibus iris,Cum decore atque omni me orbatum laude recordor. num manus adfecta recte est, cum in tumore est, aut num aliud quodpiam membrum tumidum ac turgidum non vitiose se habet?
passages.english:
And so Dionysius of Heraclea argues not unskilfully against the complaint Achilles makes in Homer, in this way, I think:
And my heart swells deep within with bitter anger,
when I recall that I have been robbed of honour and all praise.
Is a hand in a sound condition when it is swollen, or is any other limb that is swollen and puffed up not in a faulty state?

passages.original: poëta ius suum tenuit et dixit audacius)—cadit igitur in eundem et misereri et invidere. nam qui dolet rebus alicuius adversis, idem alicuius etiam secundis dolet, ut Theophrastus interitum deplorans Callisthenis sodalis sui, rebus Alexandri prosperis angitur, itaque dicit Callisthenem incidisse in hominem summa potentia summaque fortuna, sed ignarum quem ad modum rebus secundis uti conveniret.
passages.english: the poet kept to his own right and spoke rather boldly)—therefore both pitying and envying fall to the same person. For he who grieves at someone's adversity also grieves at someone's prosperity; thus Theophrastus, lamenting the death of his companion Callisthenes, is tormented by the prosperity of Alexander, and so he says that Callisthenes had fallen in with a man of the highest power and the highest fortune, but ignorant of how it was fitting to use prosperity.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening parenthesis closes a remark about a poet whose start is not given.

passages.original: quod autem Theseus a docto se audisse dicit, id de se ipso loquitur Euripides. fuerat enim auditor Anaxagorae, quem ferunt nuntiata morte filii dixisse: sciebam me genuisse mortalem. quae vox declarat is esse haec acerba, quibus non fuerint cogitata. ergo id quidem non dubium, quin omnia, quae mala putentur, sint inprovisa graviora.
passages.english: What Theseus says he heard from a learned man, Euripides says of himself. For he had been a pupil of Anaxagoras, who, they say, when the death of his son was announced, said: "I knew that I had begotten a mortal." This saying shows that these things are bitter to those by whom they have not been thought about beforehand. Therefore there is no doubt about this at least, that all things which are thought evils are heavier when unforeseen.

passages.original: hic est enim ille voltus semper idem, quem dicitur Xanthippe praedicare solita in viro suo fuisse Socrate: eodem semper se vidisse exeuntem illum domo et revertentem. Nec vero ea frons erat, quae M. Crassi illius veteris, quem semel ait in omni vita risisse Lucilius, sed tranquilla et serena; sic enim accepimus. iure autem erat semper idem voltus, cum mentis, a qua is fingitur, nulla fieret mutatio. quare accipio equidem a Cyrenaicis haec arma contra casus et eventus, quibus eorum advenientes impetus diuturna praemeditatione frangantur, simulque iudico malum illud opinionis esse, non naturae;
passages.english: For this is that countenance, always the same, which Xanthippe is said to have been accustomed to proclaim in her husband Socrates: that she had always seen him with the same [face] leaving the house and returning. Nor was it the sort of brow that belonged to the elder Marcus Crassus, who, Lucilius says, laughed once in his whole life, but calm and serene; for so we have been told. And rightly was his countenance always the same, since no change took place in the mind, by which it is shaped. Therefore I for my part accept from the Cyrenaics these weapons against chances and events, by which their attacks as they come may be broken by long premeditation, and at the same time I judge that that evil belongs to opinion, not to nature;

passages.original: Iubes me bona cogitare, oblivisci malorum. diceres aliquid, et magno quidem philosopho dignum, si ea bona esse sentires, quae essent homine dignissima. Pythagoras mihi si diceret aut Socrates aut Plato:
passages.english: You bid me think of good things and forget evils. You would be saying something, and something indeed worthy of a great philosopher, if you understood those things to be goods which are most worthy of a human being. If Pythagoras said to me, or Socrates, or Plato:
passages.notes: The passage breaks off before the quoted words.

passages.original: sed traducis cogitationes meas ad voluptates. quas? corporis, credo, aut quae propter corpus vel recordatione vel spe cogitentur. num quid est aliud? rectene interpretor sententiam tuam? solent enim isti negare nos intellegere, quid dicat Epicurus.
passages.english: But you divert my thoughts to pleasures. Which ones? Those of the body, I suppose, or those which are thought of on account of the body, either by recollection or by hope. Is there anything else? Am I interpreting your view correctly? For those people usually deny that we understand what Epicurus means.

passages.original: sic perpessio ceterorum facit, ut ea quae acciderint multo minora quam quanta sint existimata, videantur. ita fit, sensim cogitantibus ut, quantum sit ementita opinio, appareat. atque hoc idem et Telamo ille declarat: ego cum genui et Theseus: futuras mecum commentabar miserias et Anaxagoras: sciebam me genuisse mortalem. hi enim omnes diu cogitantes de rebus humanis intellegebant eas nequaquam pro opinione volgi esse extimescendas. et mihi quidem videtur idem fere accidere is qui ante meditantur, quod is quibus medetur dies, nisi quod ratio quaedam sanat illos, hos ipsa natura intellecto eo quod rem continet, illud malum, quod opinatum sit esse maxumum, nequaquam esse tantum, ut vitam beatam possit evertere.
passages.english: So the endurance of others brings it about that the things which have happened seem much smaller than they were reckoned to be. Thus it comes about, as people reflect gradually, that it becomes clear how much opinion has lied. And the famous Telamon declares this same thing: "I, when I begot [them]"; and Theseus: "I used to rehearse in my mind the miseries to come"; and Anaxagoras: "I knew that I had begotten a mortal." For all these, thinking long about human affairs, understood that these things were by no means to be feared in accordance with the opinion of the crowd. And to me indeed it seems that almost the same thing happens to those who meditate beforehand as to those whom time heals, except that a kind of reasoning heals the former, and nature itself the latter, once the point that contains the matter has been understood: that that evil which was supposed to be the greatest is by no means so great that it can overturn a happy life.
passages.notes: The quotation from Telamon is abbreviated (the full line continues "...I knew they would die").

passages.original: Omnibus enim modis fulciendi sunt, qui ruunt nec cohaerere possunt propter magnitudinem aegritudinis. ex quo ipsam aegritudinem λύπην Chrysippus quasi solutionem totius hominis appellatam putat. Quae tota poterit evelli explicata, ut principio dixi, causa aegritudinis; est enim nulla alia nisi opinio et iudicium magni praesentis atque urgentis mali. itaque et dolor corporis, cuius est morsus acerrumus, perferetur spe proposita boni, et acta aetas honeste ac splendide tantam adfert consolationem, ut eos qui ita vixerint aut non attingat aegritudo aut perleviter pungat animi dolor.
passages.english: For by every means those must be propped up who are collapsing and cannot hold together because of the greatness of their distress. Hence Chrysippus thinks that distress itself was called lypē, as if a dissolution of the whole man. All of this can be torn out once the cause of distress is explained, as I said at the beginning; for it is nothing other than the opinion and judgement of a great evil present and pressing. And so even bodily pain, whose bite is sharpest, will be endured when hope of some good is set before one, and a life lived honourably and splendidly brings such consolation that distress either does not touch those who have lived so, or pain of mind stings them very lightly.
passages.notes: lypē (λύπη) is Greek for 'grief, distress'; Chrysippus' etymology connects it with lyein 'to loosen, dissolve'.

passages.original: ut licere quidvis rhetori intellegas. quae nemo probaret, nisi insitum illud in animis haberemus, omnis bonos interitu suorum quam gravissime maerere oportere. ex hoc evenit, ut in animi doloribus alii solitudines captent, ut ait Homerus de Bellerophonte: Qui miser in campis maerens errabat Aleis Ipse suum cor edens, hominum vestigia vitans; et Nioba fingitur lapidea propter aeternum, credo, in luctu silentium, Hecubam autem putant propter animi acerbitatem quandam et rabiem fingi in canem esse conversam. sunt autem alii, quos in luctu cum ipsa solitudine loqui saepe delectat, ut illa apud Ennium nutrix: Cupído cepit míseram nunc me próloqui Caelo átque terrae Médeai míserias.
passages.english: so that you may understand that a rhetorician is allowed anything. No one would approve of these things unless we had it implanted in our minds that all good people ought to grieve as deeply as possible at the death of their own. From this it happens that in sorrows of mind some seek out solitudes, as Homer says of Bellerophon: "Who wretched wandered grieving over the Aleian plains, eating his own heart, shunning the footsteps of men"; and Niobe is represented as turned to stone, because, I suppose, of her eternal silence in mourning, while Hecuba, they think, is represented as changed into a dog because of a certain bitterness and rage of mind. There are others, however, whom in mourning it often pleases to talk with solitude itself, like that nurse in Ennius: "A longing has seized me, wretched, now to tell out to heaven and earth the miseries of Medea."

passages.original: num quis igitur quicquam decernit invitus? malo quidem me quovis dignum deputem— malo se dignum deputat, nisi miser sit. vides ergo opinionis esse, non naturae malum. Quid, quos res ipsa lugere prohibet? ut apud Homerum cotidianae neces interitusque multorum sedationem maerendi adferunt, apud quem ita dicitur: Namque nimis multos atque omni luce cadentis Cernimus, ut nemo possit maerore vacare.Quo magis est aequum tumulis mandare peremptos Firmo animo et luctum lacrimis finire diurnis.
passages.english: Does anyone, then, decide anything unwillingly? "I should consider myself worthy of any evil whatever"—he considers himself worthy of evil, unless he is wretched. You see, then, that evil belongs to opinion, not to nature. What of those whom the situation itself forbids to mourn? As in Homer the daily slaughter and deaths of many bring a calming of grief; in him it is said thus: "For we see too many falling every day, so that no one could be free from grief. All the more is it right to commit the slain to the grave with a steady mind, and to end mourning with a day's tears."
passages.notes: 'nisi miser sit' is awkward; the sense seems to be 'unless he is wretched [he thinks he does not suffer what he deserves]'. The text may be compressed or corrupt.

passages.original: Idque indicatur eorum patientia, qui cum multa sint saepe perpessi, facilius ferunt quicquid accidit, obduruisseque iam sese contra fortunam arbitrantur, ut ille apud Euripidem:Si míhi nunc tristis prímum inluxissét dies Nec tam aérumnoso návigavissém salo,Essét dolendi caúsa, ut iniecto éculei Frenó repente táctu exagitantúr novo;Sed iám subactus míseriis optórpui.
passages.english: And this is shown by the endurance of those who, having often suffered many things, bear more easily whatever befalls, and think that they have now grown hardened against fortune, like that man in Euripides: "If this sad day had dawned on me for the first time, and I had not sailed so long on so troubled a sea, there would be cause for grief, as [colts] are suddenly maddened by the new touch of the bridle put on them; but now, subdued by miseries, I have grown numb."
passages.notes: 'eculei' (colts) is the reading; the construction with 'exagitantur' is loose.

passages.original: Contra dicuntur haec: quis tam demens, ut sua voluntate maereat? natura adfert dolorem, cui quidem Crantor, inquiunt, vester cedendum putat; premit enim atque instat, nec resisti potest. itaque Oileus ille apud Sophoclem, qui Telamonem antea de Aiacis morte consolatus esset, is cum audivisset de suo, fractus est. de cuius commutata mente sic dicitur: Nec véro tanta praéditus sapiéntia Quisquám est, qui aliorum aerúmnam dictis ádlevans Non ídem, cum fortúna mutata ímpetum Convértat, clade súbita frangatúr sua,Ut ílla ad alios dícta et praecepta éxcidant.
passages.english: Against this the following is said: who is so mad as to grieve of his own will? Nature brings pain, to which, they say, your Crantor thinks one must yield; for it presses and urges on, and cannot be resisted. Thus that Oileus in Sophocles, who had earlier consoled Telamon about the death of Ajax, was broken when he heard about his own [son]. Of his changed mind it is said thus: "Nor indeed is anyone endowed with such wisdom that, while relieving others' troubles with words, he is not himself, when fortune changes and turns its assault, broken by his own sudden disaster, so that those words and precepts addressed to others fall away."

passages.original: sunt qui unum officium consolantis putent malum illud omnino non esse, ut Cleanthi placet; sunt qui non magnum malum, ut Peripatetici; sunt qui abducant a malis ad bona, ut Epicurus; sunt qui satis putent ostendere nihil inopinati accidisse, ut Cyrenaici nihil mali. Chrysippus autem caput esse censet in consolando detrahere illam opinionem maerentis, qua se officio fungi putet iusto atque debito. sunt etiam qui haec omnia genera consolandi colligant—alius enim alio modo movetur—, ut fere nos in Consolatione omnia in consolationem unam coniecimus; erat enim in tumore animus, et omnis in eo temptabatur curatio. sed sumendum tempus est non minus in animorum morbis quam in corporum; ut Prometheus ille Aeschyli, cui cum dictum esset: Atquí, Prometheu, te hóc tenere exístimo,Medéri posse rátionem iracúndiae, respondit: Siquidém qui tempestívam medicinam ádmovens Non ádgravescens vólnus inlidát manu.
passages.english: There are those who think the one duty of a consoler is [to show] that the thing is not an evil at all, as Cleanthes holds; there are those [who think it is to show it is] not a great evil, as the Peripatetics; there are those who lead away from evils to goods, as Epicurus; there are those who think it enough to show that nothing unexpected has happened, as the Cyrenaics [hold] nothing evil. Chrysippus, however, thinks the chief point in consoling is to remove from the mourner that opinion by which he thinks he is performing a just and due duty. There are also those who gather all these kinds of consolation together—for one person is moved in one way, another in another—as I for my part threw them all together into one consolation in my Consolation; for my mind was in a swollen state, and every cure was tried on it. But the right moment must be chosen no less in diseases of minds than of bodies; as that Prometheus of Aeschylus, to whom it had been said: "And yet, Prometheus, I think you grasp this, that reason can heal anger," replied: "Yes, if one applies medicine at the right time, and does not bruise the worsening wound with his hand."
passages.notes: 'ut Cyrenaici nihil mali' seems garbled; perhaps 'nihil mali' belongs elsewhere or the text is corrupt. Translated literally.

passages.original: terrorem metum concutientem, ex quo fit ut pudorem rubor, terrorem pallor et tremor et dentium crepitus consequatur, timorem metum mali adpropinquantis, pavorem metum mentem loco moventem, ex quo illud Ennius:tum pavor sapientiam omnem mi exanimato expectorat, exanimationem metum subsequentem et quasi comitem pavoris, conturbationem metum excutientem cogitata, formidinem metum permanentem.
passages.english: terror, fear that shakes, from which it comes about that blushing follows shame, and pallor, trembling and chattering of teeth follow terror; dread, fear of an approaching evil; panic, fear that dislodges the mind from its place, whence that [line of] Ennius: "then panic drives all wisdom from the breast of me, out of my senses"; consternation, fear that follows on and is as it were the companion of panic; confusion, fear that shakes out one's thoughts; fright, fear that lasts.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-list of species of fear; the Latin terms (terror, timor, pavor, exanimatio, conturbatio, formido) have no exact English equivalents.

passages.original: Ipsam aegritudinem, quam nos ut taetram et inmanem beluam fugiendam diximus, non sine magna utilitate a natura dicunt constitutam, ut homines castigationibus reprehensionibus ignominiis adfici se in delicto dolerent. impunitas enim peccatorum data videtur eis qui ignominiam et infamiam ferunt sine dolore; morderi est melius conscientia. ex quo est illud e vita ductum ab Afranio: nam cum dissolutus filius: heu me miserum! tum severus pater: dum modo doleat aliquid, doleat quidlubet.
passages.english: Distress itself, which we said must be fled as a foul and monstrous beast, they say was established by nature not without great usefulness, so that people might feel pain at being subjected to chastisements, reproofs and disgraces when in the wrong. For impunity for wrongdoing seems to be granted to those who bear disgrace and infamy without pain; it is better to be bitten by conscience. From this comes that [passage] taken from life by Afranius: for when the dissolute son [says]: "Ah, wretched me!", then the stern father [replies]: "So long as he feels pain at something, let him feel pain at whatever he likes."

passages.original: quamquam in eis ipsis videmus saepe constantiam: conlocuntur, congrediuntur, quaerunt aliquid, postulant, ut magis placati quam irati esse videantur, sed in illo genere sit sane Pacideianus aliquis hoc animo, ut narrat Lucilius: Occidam illum equidem et vincam, si id quaeritis inquit,Verum illud credo fore: in os prius accipiam ipse Quam gladium in stomacho furi ac pulmonibus sisto.Odi hominem, iratus pugno, nec longius quicquam Nobis, quam dextrae gladium dum accommodet alter;Usque adeo studio atque odio illius ecferor ira; at sine hac gladiatoria iracundia videmus progredientem apud Homerum Aiacem multa cum hilaritate, cum depugnaturus esset cum Hectore;
passages.english: And yet in those very men we often see self-control: they talk together, meet, ask for something, make demands, so that they seem rather calm than angry. But in that class let there indeed be some Pacideianus with this spirit, as Lucilius tells: "I will kill him, certainly, and conquer, if that is what you ask," he says, "but I believe this will happen: I shall first take [a blow] in the face myself before I plant my sword in the scoundrel's belly and lungs. I hate the man, I fight in anger, and nothing takes longer for us than while the other fits the sword to his right hand; so far am I carried away by rage in my zeal and hatred of him." But without this gladiatorial anger we see Ajax in Homer advancing with great cheerfulness when he was about to fight it out with Hector;
passages.notes: 'in eis ipsis' refers to gladiators, from the preceding context.

passages.original: cuius, ut arma sumpsit, ingressio laetitiam attulit sociis, terrorem autem hostibus, ut ipsum Hectorem, quem ad modum est apud Homerum, toto pectore trementem provocasse ad pugnam paeniteret. atque hi conlocuti inter se, prius quam manum consererent, leniter et quiete nihil ne in ipsa quidem pugna iracunde rabioseve fecerunt. ego ne Torquatum quidem illum, qui hoc cognomen invenit, iratum existimo Gallo torquem detraxisse, nec Marcellum apud Clastidium ideo fortem fuisse, quia fuerit iratus.
passages.english: When he took up arms, his advance brought joy to his allies and terror to the enemy, so that Hector himself, as it is in Homer, trembling in his whole breast, regretted having challenged him to battle. And these men, having spoken together before they joined combat, gently and calmly, did nothing angrily or furiously even in the fight itself. I do not think that even the famous Torquatus, who acquired this surname, was angry when he stripped the torque from the Gaul, nor that Marcellus at Clastidium was brave because he was angry.
passages.notes: 'He' is Ajax, from preceding context not supplied.

passages.original: nescio, ecquid ipsi nos fortiter in re p. fecerimus: si quid fecimus, certe irati non fecimus. an est quicquam similius insaniae quam ira? quam bene Ennius initium dixit insaniae. color, vox, oculi, spiritus, inpotentia dictorum ac factorum quam partem habent sanitatis? quid Achille Homerico foedius, quid Agamemnone in iurgio? nam Aiacem quidem ira ad furorem mortemque perduxit.
passages.english: I do not know whether I myself have done anything bravely in public life: if I have done anything, I certainly did not do it in anger. Or is there anything more like madness than anger? How well Ennius called it the beginning of madness. Complexion, voice, eyes, breathing, lack of control over words and deeds: what part do they have of sanity? What was more hideous than Homer's Achilles, what than Agamemnon in the quarrel? For Ajax, indeed, anger drove to frenzy and death.

passages.original: dicamus igitur utilem insaniam? Tracta definitiones fortitudinis: intelleges eam stomacho non egere. fortitudo est igitur adfectio animi legi summae in perpetiendis rebus obtemperans vel conservatio stabilis iudicii in eis rebus quae formidolosae videntur subeundis et repellendis vel scientia rerum formidolosarum contrariarumque aut omnino neglegendarum conservans earum rerum stabile iudicium vel brevius, ut Chrysippus (nam superiores definitiones erant Sphaeri, hominis in primis bene definientis, ut putant Stoici; sunt enim omnino omnes fere similes, sed declarant communis notiones alia magis alia)—quo modo igitur Chrysippus?fortitudo est inquit scientia rerum perferendarum vel adfectio animi in patiendo ac perferendo summae legi parens sine timore. quamvis licet insectemur istos, ut Carneades solebat, metuo ne soli philosophi sint.
passages.english: Shall we then call madness useful? Examine the definitions of courage: you will see that it has no need of bad temper. Courage, then, is a disposition of the mind obedient to the supreme law in enduring things; or the steady maintaining of judgement in undergoing and repelling things that seem fearful; or knowledge of things fearful and their contraries, or of things to be wholly disregarded, which keeps a steady judgement about those things; or, more briefly, as Chrysippus [puts it] (for the preceding definitions were Sphaerus', a man especially good at defining, as the Stoics think; indeed they are all, on the whole, nearly alike, but some express our common notions more, some less) — how, then, does Chrysippus [put it]? Courage, he says, is knowledge of things to be endured, or a disposition of the mind obeying the supreme law in suffering and enduring, without fear. However much we may attack these men, as Carneades used to, I fear they may be the only philosophers.
passages.notes: 'stomacho' here means anger or irritability (the Peripatetic claim that courage needs anger).

passages.original: quae vel optimarum rerum, ut ea sunt quae profertis, sedata tamen et tranquilla esse debent. Iam aegritudinem laudare, unam rem maxime detestabilem, quorum est tandem philosophorum? at commode dixit Afranius: dum modo doleat aliquid, doleat quidlibet. dixit enim de adulescente perdito ac dissoluto, nos autem de constanti viro ac sapienti quaerimus. et quidem ipsam illam iram centurio habeat aut signifer vel ceteri, de quibus dici non necesse est, ne rhetorum aperiamus mysteria.
passages.english: which, even when they are of the very best things, such as those you put forward, ought nonetheless to be calm and tranquil. Now, to praise distress, the one thing most detestable of all — which philosophers, pray, do that? But Afranius put it aptly: 'so long as he feels pain at something, let him feel pain at anything at all.' For he said it of a ruined and dissolute young man, whereas we are inquiring about a steadfast and wise man. And indeed, let a centurion have that very anger, or a standard-bearer, or the others of whom there is no need to speak, lest we reveal the mysteries of the rhetoricians.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the antecedent of 'quae' (passions/desires) is not in the extract.

passages.original: itaque non sine causa, cum Orestem fabulam doceret Euripides, primos tris versus revocasse dicitur Socrates: Neque tám terribilis úlla fando orátio est,Nec fórs nec ira caélitum invectúm malum,Quod nón natura humána patiendo écferat. est autem utilis ad persuadendum ea quae acciderint ferri et posse et oportere enumeratio eorum qui tulerunt.
passages.english: So it is not without reason that, when Euripides was producing the Orestes, Socrates is said to have called for the first three lines to be repeated: "There is no speech so terrible to tell, nor chance, nor evil brought on by the anger of the gods, that human nature cannot bear it out by enduring." And useful for persuading [someone] that what has happened both can and must be borne is a recounting of those who have borne it.

passages.original: cur neque deformem adulescentem quisquam amat neque formosum senem? mihi quidem haec in Graecorum gymnasiis nata consuetudo videtur, in quibus isti liberi et concessi sunt amores. bene ergo Ennius:Flágiti princípium est nudare ínter civis córpora. qui ut sint, quod fieri posse video, pudici, solliciti tamen et anxii sunt, eoque magis, quod se ipsi continent et coërcent.
passages.english: Why does no one love either an ugly youth or a handsome old man? To me, at least, this custom seems to have been born in the gymnasia of the Greeks, in which those loves are free and permitted. Well therefore [said] Ennius: "The beginning of disgrace is to bare bodies among citizens." Even if these [loves] are chaste, which I see can happen, they are nevertheless troubled and anxious, and all the more so because they restrain and hold themselves in check.

passages.original: atque, ut muliebris amores omittam, quibus maiorem licentiam natura concessit, quis aut de Ganymedi raptu dubitat, quid poëtae velint, aut non intellegit, quid apud Euripidem et loquatur et cupiat Laius? quid denique homines doctissimi et summi poëtae de se ipsis et carminibus edunt et cantibus? fortis vir in sua re p. cognitus quae de iuvenum amore scribit Alcaeus! nam Anacreontis quidem tota poësis est amatoria. maxume vero omnium flagrasse amore Reginum Ibycum apparet ex scriptis. Atque horum omnium lubidinosos esse amores videmus: philosophi sumus exorti, et auctore quidem nostro Platone, quem non iniuria Dicaearchus accusat, qui amori auctoritatem tribueremus.
passages.english: And, to pass over the loves of women, to which nature has granted greater licence, who either doubts what the poets mean by the rape of Ganymede, or does not understand what Laius in Euripides both says and desires? What, finally, do the most learned men and the greatest poets publish about themselves, both in their poems and in their songs? What things Alcaeus, a man known for his bravery in his own state, writes about the love of young men! As for Anacreon, his whole poetry is erotic. But it is clear from his writings that Ibycus of Rhegium burned with love most of all. And we see that the loves of all these men are lustful. We philosophers have arisen, and indeed on the authority of our own Plato, whom Dicaearchus accuses not without reason, to grant love authority.
passages.notes: 're p.' is the abbreviation for 're publica' (state). The final sentence is compressed: 'we philosophers have arisen ... to grant love authority' renders the relative clause of purpose 'qui ... tribueremus'.

passages.original: ergo ut constantia scientiae, sic perturbatio erroris est. Qui autem natura dicuntur iracundi aut misericordes aut invidi aut tale quid, ei sunt constituti quasi mala valetudine animi, sanabiles tamen, ut Socrates dicitur: cum multa in conventu vitia conlegisset in eum Zopyrus, qui se naturam cuiusque ex forma perspicere profitebatur, derisus est a ceteris, qui illa in Socrate vitia non agnoscerent, ab ipso autem Socrate sublevatus, cum illa sibi sic nata, sed ratione a se deiecta diceret.
passages.english: Therefore, as steadiness belongs to knowledge, so disturbance belongs to error. Those, however, who are said to be irascible by nature, or compassionate, or envious, or anything of the kind, are constituted as if with a bad health of the mind, yet they are curable, as is said of Socrates. When Zopyrus, who professed to discern each person's nature from his appearance, had heaped up many vices against him in a gathering, he was laughed at by the others, who did not recognise those vices in Socrates; but he was supported by Socrates himself, who said that those vices were indeed born in him, but had been cast out by him through reason.

passages.original: nec vero Atlans sustinere caelum nec Prometheus adfixus Caucaso nec stellatus Cepheus cum uxore genero filia traderetur, nisi caelestium divina cognitio nomen eorum ad errorem fabulae traduxisset. a quibus ducti deinceps omnes, qui in rerum contemplatione studia ponebant, sapientes et habebantur et nominabantur, idque eorum nomen usque ad Pythagorae manavit aetatem. quem, ut scribit auditor Platonis Ponticus Heraclides, vir doctus in primis, Phliuntem ferunt venisse, eumque cum Leonte, principe Phliasiorum, docte et copiose disseruisse quaedam. cuius ingenium et eloquentiam cum admiratus esset Leon, quaesivisse ex eo, qua maxime arte confideret;
passages.english: Nor indeed would Atlas be handed down [in story] as holding up the sky, nor Prometheus as fastened to the Caucasus, nor Cepheus as set among the stars with his wife, son-in-law and daughter, had not a divine knowledge of the heavenly bodies carried their name over into the error of myth. Led on by them, all who in succession devoted their efforts to the contemplation of nature were both considered and called wise men, and that name of theirs lasted right down to the age of Pythagoras. He, as Heraclides of Pontus, a pupil of Plato and a man of the first rank in learning, writes, is said to have come to Phlius and to have discussed certain matters learnedly and at length with Leon, the leading man of the Phliasians. And when Leon had admired his talent and eloquence, he asked him in what art he chiefly put his confidence;

passages.original: si vitae modum actionemque quaerimus, alterius mens rationibus agitandis exquirendisque alebatur cum oblectatione sollertiae, qui est unus suavissimus pastus animorum, alterius in caede et iniuriis cum et diurno et nocturno metu. age confer Democritum Pythagoram, Anaxagoram: quae regna, quas opes studiis eorum et delectationibus antepones?
passages.english: If we look into their manner of life and conduct, the mind of the one was nourished by working out and investigating reasonings, with the delight of ingenuity, which is the single sweetest food of minds; that of the other in slaughter and injustices, with fear both by day and by night. Come, compare Democritus, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras: what kingdoms, what riches will you rank above their studies and delights?
passages.notes: The 'one' is Archimedes (the mathematician of the context) and the 'other' the tyrant Dionysius, as the preceding context implies.

passages.original: Sunt autem haec de finibus, ut opinor, retentae defensaeque sententiae: primum simplices quattuor, nihil bonum nisi honestum, ut Stoici, nihil bonum nisi voluptatem, ut Epicurus, nihil bonum nisi vacuitatem doloris, ut Hieronymus, nihil bonum nisi naturae primis bonis aut omnibus aut maxumis frui, ut Carneades contra Stoicos disserebat.
passages.english: These, I think, are the views about the ends [of goods] that have been held and defended: first, four simple ones: nothing is good but what is honourable, as the Stoics [hold]; nothing is good but pleasure, as Epicurus [holds]; nothing is good but freedom from pain, as Hieronymus [holds]; nothing is good but to enjoy the primary goods of nature, either all or the greatest of them, as Carneades used to argue against the Stoics.

passages.original: Vides, credo, ut Epicurus cupiditatum genera diviserit, non nimis fortasse subtiliter, utiliter tamen:
passages.english: You see, I think, how Epicurus divided the kinds of desires, not perhaps very precisely, but usefully:

passages.original: tum intelleges, qui voluptatem maxime sequantur, eos minime consequi, iucunditatemque victus esse in desiderio, non in satietate. Timotheum, clarum hominem Athenis et principem civitatis, ferunt, cum cenavisset apud Platonem eoque convivio admodum delectatus esset vidissetque eum postridie, dixisse: vestrae quidem cenae non solum in praesentia, sed etiam postero die iucundae sunt. quid quod ne mente quidem recte uti possumus multo cibo et potione completi?
passages.english: Then you will understand that those who pursue pleasure most attain it least, and that the pleasantness of living lies in desire, not in satiety. They say that Timotheus, a famous man at Athens and a leading man of the state, when he had dined with Plato and been greatly delighted by that dinner party, and had seen him the next day, said: 'Your dinners are pleasant not only at the time but also on the following day.' What of the fact that we cannot even use our minds properly when stuffed with much food and drink?

passages.original: ex quo Sardanapalli, opulentissimi Syriae regis, error adgnoscitur, qui incidi iussit in busto:Haec habeo, quae edi, quaeque exsaturata libido Hausit; at illa iacent multa et praeclara relicta.quid aliud inquit Aristoteles in bovis, non in regis sepulcro inscriberes? haec habere se mortuum dicit, quae ne vivus quidem diutius habebat quam fruebatur.
passages.english: From this the error of Sardanapallus, the wealthiest king of Syria, is recognised, who ordered to be carved on his tomb: 'These I have, what I ate and what sated lust drank in; but those many splendid things lie left behind.' 'What else,' says Aristotle, 'would you inscribe on the tomb of an ox, not of a king?' He says that he has in death those things which even while alive he had no longer than he was enjoying them.

passages.original: vide ne plus commendatio in vulgus et haec, quae expetitur, gloria molestiae habeat quam voluptatis. leviculus sane noster Demosthenes, qui illo susurro delectari se dicebat aquam ferentis mulierculae, ut mos in Graecia est, insusurrantisque alteri: hic est ille Demosthenes. quid hoc levius? at quantus orator! sed apud alios loqui videlicet didicerat, non multum ipse secum.
passages.english: Consider whether popularity with the crowd and this glory that is sought after do not bring more trouble than pleasure. Our Demosthenes was rather trivial, surely, who said he was delighted by that whisper of a woman carrying water, as is the custom in Greece, and whispering to another: 'This is the famous Demosthenes.' What could be more trivial than this? Yet what an orator! But evidently he had learned to speak before others, not much with himself.

passages.original: intellegendum est igitur nec gloriam popularem ipsam per sese expetendam nec ignobilitatem extimescendam. veni Athenas inquit Democritus neque me quisquam ibi adgnovit. constantem hominem et gravem, qui glorietur a gloria se afuisse! an tibicines ique, qui fidibus utuntur, suo, non multitudinis arbitrio cantus numerosque moderantur, vir sapiens multo arte maiore praeditus non quid verissimum sit, sed quid velit vulgus, exquiret?
passages.english: It must be understood, therefore, that neither is popular glory to be sought for its own sake nor obscurity to be feared. 'I came to Athens,' says Democritus, 'and nobody there recognised me.' A steady and serious man, who boasts that he kept away from glory! Or shall flute-players and those who play the lyre regulate their songs and rhythms by their own judgement, not the crowd's, while the wise man, endowed with a far greater art, seeks out not what is truest but what the mob wants?

passages.original: an quicquam stultius quam, quos singulos sicut operarios barbarosque contemnas, eos aliquid putare esse universos? ille vero nostras ambitiones levitatesque contemnet honoresque populi etiam ultro delatos repudiabit; nos autem eos nescimus, ante quam paenitere coepit, contemnere. est apud Heraclitum physicum de principe Ephesiorum Hermodoro;
passages.english: Or is anything more foolish than to think that those whom individually you despise as labourers and barbarians are something when taken all together? He [the wise man] indeed will despise our ambitions and frivolities and will reject the honours of the people even when offered unasked; we, however, do not know how to despise them before we have begun to regret [them]. There is [a passage] in Heraclitus the natural philosopher about Hermodorus, the leading man of the Ephesians;
passages.notes: 'paenitere coepit' is impersonal (lit. 'before it has begun to repent [us]').

passages.original: aut enim fruatur aliquis pariter cum aliis voluptate potandi aut, ne sobrius in violentiam vinolentorum incidat, ante discedat. sic iniurias fortunae, quas ferre nequeas, defugiendo relinquas. Haec eadem, quae Epicurus, totidem verbis dicit Hieronymus.
passages.english: For either one should enjoy the pleasure of drinking equally with the others, or, lest when sober he run into the violence of the drunken, he should leave first. So you may escape the injuries of fortune which you cannot bear by fleeing from them. These same things that Epicurus says, Hieronymus says in as many words.
